slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> are dinucleotides containing one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NIACINAMIDE">nicotinamide</a> base and one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENINE">adenine</a> base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety.
<p>
These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cofactors" title="An enzyme cofactor is a non-protein chemical compound that is required by an enzyme for catalysis of a chemical reaction. Cofactors associate with inactive <i>apo</i>-enzymes, resulting in formation of active <i>holo</i>-enzymes.&#10;Unlike cosubstrates, the cofactors are restored to their original state at the end of the catalytic cycle and are thus not included in the reaction equation.&#10;&#10;Cofactors can be inorganic ions (e.g. Ca<sup>2+</sup>), inorganic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>an iron-sulfur cluster</a>) or organic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE''>pyridoxal 5'-phosphate</a>). Some compounds may act as cofactors for a particular enzyme and a cosubstrate for a different enzyme, depending on whether they are restored to their active state at the end of the reaction. &#10;Cofactors that are tightly bound to an enzyme have often been referred to as prosthetic groups. It should be noted that the degree of tightness required for this definition has not been defined, and that the same cofactor may bind differently to different enzymes, making this term imprecise. Thus, it is recommended not to use it. Organic cofactors that are loosely bound to the enzyme have been often referred to as coenzymes. However, that term is also imprecise, and it is recommended not to use it either.">cofactors</a>.  They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes".
<p>
The most common function of  <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADH">NADH</a>, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form.
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADPH">NADPH</a>, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a>, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> is reduced by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-84">photosystem I</a>. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative branch) I</a>).</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PHENYLACETATE">Phenylacetate</a> is a major intermediate in bacterial degradation of many aromatic compounds [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11260461">Luengo01</a>]. Microbes can oxidize phenylacetate under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see also <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-1341">phenylacetate degradation II (anaerobic)</a>), and the first step in both pathways is the same - the activition of phenylacetate to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-207">phenylacetyl-CoA</a> by a <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-12132">phenylacetate-CoA ligase</a>.
<p>
Despite the fact that the existence of an aerobic pathway was reported back in 1955 [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bKunita55%5d">Kunita55</a>], the exact chemistry, which is unusual for an aerobic pathway, was solved only in 2010 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>]. All of the pathway's intermediates remain in the form of CoA-thioesters, a characteristic typical of anaerobic degradation pathways. 
<p>
De-aromatization of the ring is achieved by activation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-207">phenylacetyl-CoA</a> to a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2362">2-(1,2-epoxy-1,2-dihydrophenyl)acetyl-CoA</a>, catalyzed by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-8168">ring 1,2-phenylacetyl-CoA epoxidase</a>, a multicomponent oxygenase. The reactive non-aromatic epoxide is then isomerized to a seven-member <i>o</i>-heterocyclic enol ether, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2363">2-oxepin-2(3H)-ylideneacetyl-CoA</a>, and the ring is cleaved. The rest of the pathway consists of &beta;-oxidation steps leading to formation of the TCA cycle intermediates <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=SUC-COA">succinyl-CoA</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17259607">Nogales07</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">AtoB is one of two 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolases in <i>E. coli</i>.  While <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=FADA-MONOMER">FadA</a> has broad substrate specificity, AtoB is strictly specific for acetoacetyl-CoA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/236278">Feigenbaum75</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9904">Duncombe76</a>].
<p>
Crystal structures of AtoB alone and in a complex with CoA have been solved; the structure can be described as a loosely interacting dimer of tight dimers [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27380370">Ithayaraja16</a>].  The gene for this study was cloned from <i>E. coli</i> BL21 (DE3), but the sequence is identical to that of the K-12 protein.
<p>
AtoB expression is induced by growth on acetoacetate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4563344">Pauli72</a>].
<p>
AtoB is used for metabolic engineering of 1-butanol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21398484">Shen11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25866563">Menon15</a>] and medium-chain fuel [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25645093">Kim15d</a>] production.
<p>
AtoB: "<b>a</b>ce<b>to</b>acetate" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4563344">Pauli72</a>]</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase is a key enzyme present in all three kingdoms of life. In humans, it is a mitochondrial protein, and defficiency in its activity results in the disease glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1), a relatively common cause
of acute metabolic brain damage in infants [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11787045">Goodman01</a>].
<p>
Glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase is a dual function enzyme, which also catalyzes the reaction of glutaconyl-CoA decarboxylase, resulting in crotonyl-CoA. Glutaconyl-CoA is an intermediate in the overall oxidative decarboxylation of glutaryl-CoA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8439237">Hartel93</a>].
<p>
The enzymes express at high level when cells of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-286"><i>Pseudomonas</i></a> strains KB 740 and K 172 were grown on benzoate or other aromatic compounds under anaerobic conditions. Similar activity was also detected in cell-free extracts of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1073"><i>Rhodopseudomonas</i></a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1068"><i>Rhodomicrobium</i></a> and <i> Rhodocyclus</i> after phototrophic growth on benzoate.
<p>
Enzymes have been purified from the two <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-286"><i>Pseudomonas</i></a> strains, and were found to be very similar. Both were homotetramers with a molecular weight of 170 kDa, and contained 1 mol of FAD per subunit [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8439237">Hartel93</a>].
<p>
The bi-functional glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenases that depend on ETF (electron-transfer flavoprotein) form one class of glutaconyl-CoA decarboxylases. A second class of these enzymes exists which depends on biotin rather than FAD.
Enzymes that belong to the other class have been purified from glutamate fermenting bacteria (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-7.2.4.5">EC 7.2.4.5, glutaconyl-CoA decarboxylase</a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2244788">Beatrix90</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Crotonase is an enzyme in the central fermentation pathway of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1488"><i>Clostridium acetobutylicum</i></a> that plays a central role in the production of both acids and solvents. 
The enzyme been purified to homogeneity from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1488"><i>Clostridium acetobutylicum</i></a> and found to be a homotetramer. The enzyme was highly specific for short, C4-C6, chain length substrates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5057466">Waterson72</a>]. The enzyme exhibits an extremely high turnover number for <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CROTONYL-COA">crotonyl-CoA</a> (Vmax = 6.5 x 10<sup>6</sup> mol per minute per mole of enzyme), and is markedly sensitive to inhibition by crotonyl-CoA at concentrations greater than about 75 &mu;M [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7024731">Waterson81</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-98">crt</a> gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned and sequenced [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8655474">Boynton96</a>].
While earlier work reported that the subunit size is 43 kDa, and thus that the protein is a homotetramer [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5057466">Waterson72</a>], the size of the recombinant monomer was found to be 29 kDa [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8655474">Boynton96</a>], and thus the protein is most likely a hexamer, similar to the bovine enzyme.</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Catabolic enoyl-CoA hydratases (ECHs) are important enzymes whose best known role is participation in the &beta;-oxidation pathway of fatty acids. ECH catalyzes the second step, the hydration of a <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA">a (2<i>E</i>)-2-enoyl-CoA</a> to a <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=L-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=ACYL-COA''>Acyl-CoAs</a> are oxoacids that have been activated by <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CO-A''>coenzyme A</a>. They are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety.&#10;&#10;<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs''>Medium-chain acyl-CoAs</a>  are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 6-12 carbons.&#10;&#10;<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs''>Long-chain acyl-CoAs</a> are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 13-21 carbons.&#10;&#10;<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA''>Very long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs</a> are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 22 carbons or longer.">a 2,3,4-saturated (3<i>S</i>)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA</a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=FAO-PWY">fatty acid &beta;-oxidation I (generic)</a>).
<p>
Two types of catabolic ECH enzymes are known: the peroxisomal ECHs, as well as bacterial enzymes such as the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> FadB, are parts of multifunctional complexes that have three or four activities, including ECH [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3286611">Yang88</a>]. The mitochondrial enzymes, on the other hand, are homohexameric, single function enzymes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12467702">Agnihotri03</a>]. Analogs of the mitochondrial enzyme have been discovered in bacteria. For example, two such enzymes, one of which homodimeric, were described in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1772"><i>Mycolicibacterium smegmatis</i></a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7451404">Fujita80</a>]. A gene homologous to the mitochondrial ECH was discovered in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1061"><i>Rhodobacter capsulatus</i></a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1743516">Beckman91</a>] and homologous genes are present in many bacteria.
<p>
Although mammalian ECH enzymes have been studied extensively (for review, see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12467702">Agnihotri03</a>]), surprisingly little is known about the bacterial catabolic enzymes (more is known about the bacterial biosynthetic enzymes involved in lipid or polyhydroxyalkanoate biosynthesis - see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10713420">Tsuge00</a>] and [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12115060">Fiedler02</a>]).
<p>
An ECH enzyme involved in the catabolism of branched-chain amino acids has been characterized and partially purified from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-303"><i>Pseudomonas putida</i></a> by Conrad et al [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4150713">Conrad74</a>]. The enzyme was induced during growth on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ILE">L-isoleucine</a>, and active with both <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CROTONYL-COA">crotonyl-CoA</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1083">(<i>E</i>)-2-methylcrotonoyl-CoA</a>, but not with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=TRANS-3-METHYL-GLUTACONYL-COA">3-methylglutaconyl-CoA</a>, suggesting it may not be involved in <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=LEU">L-leucine</a> degradation. The enzyme was further characterized by Roberts et al, who found that the enzyme was most active with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CROTONYL-COA">crotonyl-CoA</a>, had significant activity with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1083">(<i>E</i>)-2-methylcrotonoyl-CoA</a> and rather low activity with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA">3-methylcrotonyl-CoA</a>, another intermediate in <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=LEU">L-leucine</a> degradation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/678016">Roberts78</a>]. They concluded that the enzyme participates in both fatty acid oxidation and the metabolism of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ILE">L-isoleucine</a>, and potentially also in the degradation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=VAL">L-valine</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/678016">Roberts78</a>].
<p>
A <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-11695">similar enzyme</a> was described by Puukka in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-294"><i>Pseudomonas fluorescens</i></a> during growth on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=VAL">L-valine</a>, that converted <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHACRYLYL-COA">methylacrylyl-CoA</a> to <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=3-HYDROXY-ISOBUTYRYL-COA">3-hydroxy-isobutanoyl-CoA</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4633993">Puukka73</a>]. It is not known if that enzyme was also involved in the degradation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ILE">L-isoleucine</a> since its specificity has not been characterized. However, it was best induced by growth on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ILE">L-isoleucine</a>.</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-11936">(<i>S</i>)-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase</a> (BHBD) is one of the enzymes in the central fermentation pathway of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1520"><i>Clostridium beijerinckii</i></a>. It catalyzes the first committed step in the production of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BUTYRIC_ACID">butanoate</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BUTANOL">butan-1-ol</a>.
<p>
BHBD enzymes can be specific for either the (<i>R</i>) or (<i>S</i>) isomers of 3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA, and can be either NADH- or NADPH-dependent [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19304817">Tseng09</a>]. The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-97">hbd</a>-encoded enzyme from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1520"><i>Clostridium beijerinckii</i></a> is (<i>S</i>)-specific, and has higher processivity using NADH [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1444364">Colby92</a>].
<p>
An NADPH-dependent <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13586">(<i>R</i>)-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase</a> has been characterized from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1063"><i>Cereibacter sphaeroides</i></a>. That enzyme is encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-10357">phaB</a> gene [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16856937">Alber06</a>]. The bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-381666"><i>Cupriavidus necator</i> H16</a> appears to possess both enzymes [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bHaywood88%5d">Haywood88</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells contain multiple forms of acetyl-coA acetyltransferases, both
biosynthetic and catabolic.
In general, catabolic forms, such as those involved in fatty acid &beta;-oxidation, show broad specificity
for <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CO-A">coenzyme A</a>-initiated thiolysis of &beta;-ketoacyl-CoAs, and would accept a wide range of
substrates, with  chain length of C<sub>4</sub> to C<sub>16</sub> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5177">glutaryl-CoA degradation</a>
and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=FAO-PWY">fatty acid &beta;-oxidation I (generic)</a>).
<p>
On the other hand, biosynthetic forms usually have narrow specificity for acetoacetyl-CoA, and are
involved in several biosynthetic pathways, such as ketone body utilization, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-922">mevalonate pathway I (eukaryotes and bacteria)</a>,
and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY1-3">polyhydroxybutanoate biosynthesis</a>.
<p>
The biosynthetic thiolases are able to generate a carbon-carbon bond by a condensation reaction,
even though the equilibrium lies far in the direction of thiolysis. When condensation occurs,
the enzymes treat two identical acetyl-coA molecules differentially, using one as a C-2 carbanion
equivalent, and the other as an electrophile at C-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2670935">Peoples89</a>].
<p>
The enzyme from the facultative chemolithoautotrophic bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-106590"><i>Cupriavidus necator</i></a> was purified
49-fold [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4198758">Oeding73</a>].
The cleavage reaction is characterized by substrate inhibition by acetoacetyl-CoA,
which is partially relieved by free CoA. On the other hand, the condensation reaction is competitively
inhibited by free CoA. The optimum pH for the cleavage reaction is 8.1, and that for the condensation
reaction is 7.8.
Hill plots indicate two acetoacetyl-CoA-binding sites [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4198758">Oeding73</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-9968">phbA</a> gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned and expressed in
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3049530">Slater88</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2848014">Schubert88</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2670935">Peoples89</a>].
<p>
</comment>

slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7788">Acetyl-CoA <i>C</i>-acetyltransferase</a> was purified and characterized from the extremely halophilic archaeon <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-157834"><i>Halobacterium</i> sp. <i>JP-6</i></a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12013440">Liu02a</a>].
<p>
The native enzyme had a molecular mass of 80 kDa, and consisted of two identical subunits of 43kDa each. The purified enzyme had a very narrow optimal pH range around of 7.9 for acetoacetyl-CoA thiolysis. The thiolytic activity was inhibited by the presence of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=MG%2b2">Mg<SUP>2+</SUP></a> -at 20mM only 40% of the activity remained. On the other hand, the enzyme was stimulated by KCl or NaCl.
<p>
The distinct kinetic profile of the enzyme indicates that it may have a different catalytic mechanism from the so-called ping-pong mechanism employed by other thiolases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12013440">Liu02a</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FAD">Flavin adenine dinucleotide</a> (FAD) is an important redox cofactor involved in many reactions in metabolism. The fully oxidized form, FAD, is converted to the reduced form, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FADH2">FADH<SUB>2</SUB></a> by receiving two electrons and two protons. The reduced form can be oxidized to a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FADH">semireduced form</a> (semiquinone, FADH) by donating one electron and one proton. The semiquinone is then oxidized back to the fully oxidized form by losing a second electron and proton.
Even though FAD has an aromatic ring system, FADH2 does not, making it significantly higher in energy.
<p>
Many proteins contain a flavin moiety, either in the form of FAD or <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FMN">FMN</a>. They are known as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Flavoproteins">flavoproteins</a>.</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.3.8.6">EC 1.3.8.6, glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (ETF)</a>, which is encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G1G01-166">gcdH</a> gene, is a key enzyme in the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5177">glutaryl-CoA degradation</a> pathway.
<p>
Two enzymes in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-160488"><i>Pseudomonas putida</i> KT2440</a> can act on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARATE">glutarate</a> - <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G1G01-166">gcdH</a>, which encodes <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.3.8.6">EC 1.3.8.6, glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (ETF)</a>, and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G1G01-3088">csiD</a>, which encodes <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.14.11.64">EC 1.14.11.64, glutarate dioxygenase</a>. Inactivation of each gene alone does not result in a strong phenotype. However, inactivation of both genes results in a mutant that is incapable of using <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARATE">glutarate</a> as its sole carbon source [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29844506">Zhang18b</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-10356">phaA</a> gene of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1063"><i>Cereibacter sphaeroides</i></a> was identified by generating transposon mutants
that were defective in acetate metabolism. 
The disrupted gene was very similar to biosynthetic &beta;-ketothiolase from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-350"><i>Zoogloea ramigera</i></a>,
suggesting that it encodes a <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13585">acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase</a>.
This functional assignment was verified by the fact that the mutant was able to grow on
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=3-KETOBUTYRATE">acetoacetate</a> but not on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16856937">Alber06</a>].
<p>
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">In the initial study of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5789">3-hydroxypropanoate/4-hydroxybutanate cycle</a> enzymes this enzyme has not been purified from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-43687"><i>Metallosphaera sedula</i></a>. The two enzymatic activities (later found to be catalyzed by a single enzyme) were measured in cell-free extracts. The crotonyl-CoA hydratase activity, in particular, was extremely high [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18079405">Berg07</a>]. 
<p>
In a later study, a search of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-43687"><i>Metallosphaera sedula</i></a> genome revealed a gene (<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-15030">Msed_0399</a>) that encodes a fusion protein, composed of an enoyl-CoA hydratase C-terminal domain (~20 kDa) and a dehydrogenase N-terminal domain (~40 kDa). The expected bifunctional hydratase/dehydrogenase activity was confirmed to occur in similar amounts in extracts of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-43687"><i>Metallosphaera sedula</i></a>, and the protein was purified more than 63-fold to near homogeneity. Mass-spectrometric analysis identified the 70-kDa protein as the product of <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-15030">Msed_0399</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21169482">RamosVera11</a>]. 
<p>
The gene was subsequently cloned and expressed in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, and the recombinant protein was purified. Biochemical characterization of the purified recombinant protein confirmed both predicted activities [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21169482">RamosVera11</a>].
<p>
The gene was later cloned (without a His tag) and produced recombinantly in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, along with the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-10489">hbs</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-10490">hbd</a>, and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-15031">Msed_0656</a> genes, which together catalyze the 4 last steps of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5789">3-hydroxypropanoate/4-hydroxybutanate cycle</a>. The predicted combined action of the four enzymes is the conversion of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=4-HYDROXY-BUTYRATE">4-hydroxybutanoate</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a>. Indeed, when the four recombinant proteins were combined <i>in vitro</i> they were able to catalyze this conversion [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24532060">Hawkins14</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">This enzyme has not been purified from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-43687"><i>Metallosphaera sedula</i></a> in the initial study of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5789">3-hydroxypropanoate/4-hydroxybutanate cycle</a> enzymes. Although the activity was measured in cell-free extracts, the identity of the gene encoding it was not known at the time [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18079405">Berg07</a>]. 
<p>
In a later study, a search of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-43687"><i>Metallosphaera sedula</i></a> genome revealed a gene (<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-15031">Msed_0656</a>) that was highly similar to eubacterial &beta;-ketothiolase enzymes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21169482">RamosVera11</a>]. While the enzyme from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-43687"><i>Metallosphaera sedula</i></a> was not purified at the time, the homologous gene from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-444157"><i>Pyrobaculum neutrophilum</i> V24Sta</a> (<i>Tneu_0249</i>) was cloned and expressed as a soluble, N-terminal His<sub>10</sub>-tagged protein in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>. The purified recombinant enzyme catalyzed the expected thiolytic cleavage of acetoacetyl-CoA into two molecules of acetyl-CoA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21169482">RamosVera11</a>].
<p>
The gene from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-43687"><i>Metallosphaera sedula</i></a> was later cloned with an N-terminal His<sub>6</sub> tag and produced recombinantly in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, along with the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-10489">hbs</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-10490">hbd</a>, and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-15030">Msed_0399</a> genes, which together catalyze the 4 last steps of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5789">3-hydroxypropanoate/4-hydroxybutanate cycle</a>. The predicted combined action of the four enzymes is the conversion of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=4-HYDROXY-BUTYRATE">4-hydroxybutanoate</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a>. Indeed, when the four recombinant proteins were combined <i>in vitro</i> they were able to catalyze this conversion [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24532060">Hawkins14</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Gram-positive cocci, such as the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-90964"><i>Staphylococcaceae</i></a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1300"><i>Streptococcaceae</i></a>, and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-81852"><i>Enterococcaceae</i></a>, possess the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-922">mevalonate pathway</a> rather than the more commn <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=NONMEVIPP-PWY">methylerythritol phosphate pathway I</a>. The pathway genes, which are highly divergent from those of mammals, are believed to have been horizontally transferred from a primitive eukaryotic cell.
<p>
Enterococci uniquely encode a bifunctional protein, encoded by the <i>mvaE</i> gene, that catalyzes both <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.3.1.9">EC 2.3.1.9, acetyl-CoA <em>C</em>-acetyltransferase</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.1.1.34">EC 1.1.1.34, hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA reductase (NADPH)</a> activities. Genetic disruption experiments in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1313"><i>Streptococcus pneumoniae</i></a> have shown that the gene is essential [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10894743">Wilding00</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-17752">mvaE</a> gene was cloned from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1351"><i>Enterococcus faecalis</i></a> with an N-terminal His tag and expressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11914342">Hedl02</a>]. As predicted, the purified protein catalyzed both the acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase and HMG-CoA reductase reactions.</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">During the degradation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-19011">methyl <i>tert</i>-butyl ether</a> (MTBE) the intermediate <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETOACETYL-COA">acetoacetyl-CoA</a> is potentially converted by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.3.1.9">EC 2.3.1.9, acetyl-CoA <em>C</em>-acetyltransferase</a>, to two acetyl-CoA molecules that can feed into the tricarboxylic acid cycle.
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-44561">Mpe_A3367</a> gene of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-420662"><i>Methylibium petroleiphilum</i> PM1</a>, which is located on the chromosome, is predicted to encode acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17158667">Kane07</a>]. The gene is 1.6-fold upregulated by exposure to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-19011">methyl <i>tert</i>-butyl ether</a> (MTBE), and thus was proposed to catalyze this predicted activity during MTBE degradation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17158667">Kane07</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17890343">Hristova07</a>].
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARYL-COA">Glutaryl-CoA</a> is a common intermediate in the degradation of many different compounds,
such as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOATE">benzoate</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOYLCOA">benzoyl-CoA</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=LYS">L-lysine</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=TRP">L-tryptophan</a> and many more.
In this pathway <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARYL-COA">glutaryl-CoA</a> is degraded by &beta;-oxidation to 2 molecules of
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a> and one molecule of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>.
<p>
This pathway can operate under both anaerobic [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8436125">Koch93</a>] and aerobic conditions
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11705404">Westover01</a>], although the enzymes catalyzing it may be specialized for either aerobic
or anaerobic operation.</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=THLCLOS-MONOMER">Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase</a> catalyzes the condensation of two <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a> molecules to form <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETOACETYL-COA">acetoacetyl-CoA</a>. The enzyme occupies an important position in the central fermentation pathway leading to production of either acids or solvents in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1488"><i>Clostridium acetobutylicum</i></a>. It lies at the branch point of these pathways and influences the flow of carbon into them.
<p>
The enzyme from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-272562"><i>Clostridium acetobutylicum</i> ATCC 824</a> has been purified 70-fold to homogeneity. Unlike the thiolase in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1501"><i>Clostridium pasteurianum</i></a>, the thiolase from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1488"><i>Clostridium acetobutylicum</i></a> has high relative activity throughout the physiological range of internal pH of 5.5 to 7.0, indicating that change in internal pH during acid production is not an important factor in the regulation of this thiolase. The thiolase is inhibited by micromolar levels of CoA, and by ATP and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BUTYRYL-COA">butanoyl-CoA</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16347774">Wiesenborn88</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-96">thl</a> gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned by using primary antibodies raised to the purified enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1685080">Petersen91a</a>] and subsequently sequenced [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867955">StimHerndon95</a>].
<p>
Thiolase may also play an indirect role in acid uptake during solventogenesis</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Like the cyclohyrolase from methanogenic archaea, the methenyl-H<sub>4</sub>MPT cyclohydrolase from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-272630"><i>Methylorubrum extorquens</i> AM1</a> is specific for H<sub>4</sub>MPT, catalyzes the formation of the <i>N</i><sup>5</sup>-derivative, and is a monofunctional enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10215859">Pomper99</a>].
<p>
The enzyme has been purified and characterized. It is composed of two identical subunits of molecular mass 33 kDa [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10215859">Pomper99</a>]. The gene encoding the enzyme was identified via the N-terminal amino acid sequence. The sequence is approximately 40% identical to that of the orthologous enzymes from methanogenic archaea [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10215859">Pomper99</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase catalyzes a step in methanogenesis from CO2.
The enzyme contains approximately 1 mol molybdenum, 1 mol molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide, 30 mol non-heme iron and 30 mol sulfur per mol enzyme. Tungsten can not substitute for molybdenum  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8617280">Vorholt96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2125267">Karrasch90</a>, <a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bArchMicro161-528%5d">Schmitz94</a>, <a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bFerry93%5d">Ferry93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9782487">Thauer98</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.2.7.12">EC 1.2.7.12, formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase</a>, catalyzes the reversible conversion of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Methanofurans" title="Methanofurans are a group of related carbon-carrier cofactors involved in the first step of the methanogenic reduction of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE''>CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> (see <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHANOGENESIS-PWY''>methanogenesis from H<SUB>2</SUB> and CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>). Methanofurans react with <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE''>CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> to form the carbamate <i>N</i>-carboxymethanofuran, which is reduced to <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Formyl-methanofurans''>a formylmethanofuran</a> by <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.2.7.12''>EC 1.2.7.12, formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase</a>.&#10;&#10;In addition, the cofactor also participates at a later stage of all methanogenesis pathways. These pathways converge at the compound <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM''>methyl-CoM</a>, which is then disproportionated into <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4''>methane</a> and <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE''>CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>; the latter process involves methanofuran (see <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5209''>methyl-coenzyme M oxidation to CO<sub>2</sub></a>).&#10;&#10;Methanofuran is also used by methylotrophic bacteria as a coenzyme to oxidize formaldehyde to formate [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9651254''>Chistoserdova98</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11532013''>Pomper01</a>].&#10;&#10;Methanofurans are the only cofactors known to contain a furan moiety, although furans have been identified in polyketides and fatty acid derived natural products, and are often formed during the heating or oxidation of carbohydrates [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12013276''>Graham02</a>].&#10;&#10;The chemical structure of methanofuran varies among different methanogens. At this time (2014) five variants have been characterized:&#10;<a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17181''>methanofuran a</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-145262''><i>Methanothermobacter thermautotrophicus</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1517208''>Eisenreich92</a>], <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7628''>methanofuran b</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2208''><i>Methanosarcina barkeri</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2883935''>Bobik87</a>], <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7629''>methanofuran c</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2173''><i>Methanobrevibacter smithii</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3170480''>White88a</a>], <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=methanofuran-d''>methanofuran d</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2190''><i>Methanocaldococcus jannaschii</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24977328''>Miller14</a>] and <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17182''>methanofuran e</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-39152''><i>Methanococcus maripaludis</i></a>, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2187''><i>Methanococcus vannielii</i></a> and <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-155863''><i>Methanothermococcus okinawensis</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25203397''>Allen14</a>].&#10;&#10;All methanofurans contain the basic core structure of 4-[<i>N</i>-&gamma;-L-glutamyl-&gamma;-L-glutamyl)-<i>p</i>-(&beta;-aminoethyl)phenoxymethyl]-2-(aminomethyl)furan, but with different attached side chains.">methanofuran</a> to <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Formyl-methanofurans">formylmethanofuran</a>, an intermediate in methanogenesis from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>.
<p>
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-145262"><i>Methanothermobacter thermautotrophicus</i></a> contains two such enzymes, a <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-562">tungsten-containing enzyme</a> and a <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-561">molybdenum-containing enzyme</a>. The molybdenum enzyme, encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-348">fwdA</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-347">fmdB</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-346">fmdC</a> genes, is synthesized only when molybdenum is available in the growth medium. The tungsten enzyme, encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-348">fwdA</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-351">fwdB</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-350">fwdC</a>, and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-349">fwdD</a> genes, is synthesized when either tungsten or molybdenum is present.
<p>
The molybdenum enzyme contains molybdenum, a molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide and iron-sulfur clusters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8954165">Hochheimer96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1915887">Borner91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9342247">Vorholt97</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8125106">Bertram94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7813470">Bertram94b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9782487">Thauer98</a>].</comment>

The tungsten enzyme contains <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-21374"><i>bis</i>(guanylyl tungstenpterin) cofactor</a> and iron-sulfur clusters. If the growth
medium contains molybdenum, the tungsten enzyme will contain molybdenum instead of tungsten [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8575452">Hochheimer95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8954165">Hochheimer96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8161283">Bertram94a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9342247">Vorholt97</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8125106">Bertram94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7813470">Bertram94b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9782487">Thauer98</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">There are two methylene-H<SUB>4</SUB>MPT dehydrogenases present in
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-145262"><i>Methanothermobacter thermautotrophicus</i></a>. One form, which is encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-354">mtd</a> gene, is
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Factor-420" title="One of the distinguishing features of methanogenic bacteria is their blue-green fluorescence when irradiated with UV light.&#10;&#10;<br> This fluorescence is due to F<sub>420</sub>, a flavin-related redox-active compound that is used as a cosubstrate by many enzymes in these organisms.&#10;&#10;While it is well-known for its role in methanogenesis, factor 420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium, where it assists in the synthesis of antibiotics like tetracycline and lincomycin. In addition, a modified form of the cofactor is also used by cyanobacteria in the repair of DNA damage.&#10;.&#10;Factor 420 (F<sub>420</sub>), named for its intense absorbance at 420 nm, was originally isolated by Cheeseman et al [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5079072''>Cheeseman72</a>], and later identified by Eirich et al as the N-(N-L-lactyl-&gamma;-L-glutamyl)-L-glutamic acid phosphodiester of 7,8-didemethyl-8-hydroxy-5-deazariboflavin 5'-phosphate [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/728375''>Eirich78</a>].&#10;&#10;The <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-8112''>F<sub>420</sub> biosynthetic pathway</a> produces the intermediate <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17242''>F<sub>420</sub>-0</a>, which contains no glutamate side chains. Glutamates are then added by several enzymes. F<sub>420</sub> molecules isolated from different organisms differ in the number of the glutamate molecules in the side chains, as well as the nature of the bond (which could be either &alpha; or &gamma;) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11717263''>Choi01</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12909715''>Li03a</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12867481''>Graupner03</a>].">a factor 420</a>-dependent and oxygen-stable. The other is <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=HYDROGEN-MOLECULE">H<SUB>2</SUB></a>-forming
(or <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Factor-420" title="One of the distinguishing features of methanogenic bacteria is their blue-green fluorescence when irradiated with UV light.&#10;&#10;<br> This fluorescence is due to F<sub>420</sub>, a flavin-related redox-active compound that is used as a cosubstrate by many enzymes in these organisms.&#10;&#10;While it is well-known for its role in methanogenesis, factor 420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium, where it assists in the synthesis of antibiotics like tetracycline and lincomycin. In addition, a modified form of the cofactor is also used by cyanobacteria in the repair of DNA damage.&#10;.&#10;Factor 420 (F<sub>420</sub>), named for its intense absorbance at 420 nm, was originally isolated by Cheeseman et al [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5079072''>Cheeseman72</a>], and later identified by Eirich et al as the N-(N-L-lactyl-&gamma;-L-glutamyl)-L-glutamic acid phosphodiester of 7,8-didemethyl-8-hydroxy-5-deazariboflavin 5'-phosphate [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/728375''>Eirich78</a>].&#10;&#10;The <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-8112''>F<sub>420</sub> biosynthetic pathway</a> produces the intermediate <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17242''>F<sub>420</sub>-0</a>, which contains no glutamate side chains. Glutamates are then added by several enzymes. F<sub>420</sub> molecules isolated from different organisms differ in the number of the glutamate molecules in the side chains, as well as the nature of the bond (which could be either &alpha; or &gamma;) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11717263''>Choi01</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12909715''>Li03a</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12867481''>Graupner03</a>].">a factor 420</a>-independent), oxygen-sensitive, and is encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-355">hmd</a> gene.
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=HMDMAUTO-MONOMER">H<SUB>2</SUB>-forming methylene-H<SUB>4</SUB>MPT dehydrogenase</a> is a novel hydrogenase, which differs from other hydrogenases
in that it does not contain a chromophoric prosthetic group such as nickel and/or iron-sulfur clusters.
It is also not inhibited by CO, acetylene, NO, azide or cyanide; it does not catalyze the reduction of
dyes with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=HYDROGEN-MOLECULE">H<SUB>2</SUB></a>; and in the absence of an electron acceptor it does not 
catalyze an <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=HYDROGEN-MOLECULE">H<SUB>2</SUB></a>/<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PROTON">H<SUP>+</SUP></a> exchange. The enzyme does
contain a small amount of zinc, but it was not necessary for enzyme activity
 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1521540">Zirngibl92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7628605">Klein95a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7588769">Klein95b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8142403">Schleucher94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8383041">Schworer93</a>, <a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bFEBSLett261-112%5d">Zirngibl90</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Methanogenesis from H<i>2</i>, CO<i>2</i>, or acetate is dependent on the presence of sodium ions. The sodium ion-dependent step has been shown to be the transfer of a methyl group from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-THMPT"><i>N</i><sup>5</sup>-methyltetrahydromethanopterin</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a>. The exergonic methyl transfer reaction is coupled to the endergonic pumping of sodium ions out of the cell, forming an ion gradient across the membrane. The two processes are catalyzed by a membrane-associated Na<sup>+</sup>-translocating/methyltranferase multienzyme complex composed of eight different subunits, MtrA-H. In methanogens lacking cytochromes, the MtrA-H reaction represents the only chemiosmotic process [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11248186">Gottschalk01</a>].
<p>
Primary structure analysis predicts MtrC, MtrD and MtrE as integral membrane proteins with at least six transmembrane helices, MtrA, MtrB, MtrF and MtrG as peripheral proteins with one transmembrane helix anchor, and MtrH as a peripheral protein without a membrane anchor. The only prosthetic group  is <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7162"><i>Co</i>&alpha;-[&alpha;-(5-hydroxybenzimidazolyl)]-cob(I)amide</a>, which is is axially coordinated by a histidine residue of the MtrA subunit (His<sup>84</sup> in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-145262"><i>Methanothermobacter thermautotrophicus</i></a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898900">Harms96a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9801157">Sauer98a</a>]. During the catalytic cycle the methyl group is transferred from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-THMPT"><i>N</i><sup>5</sup>-methyltetrahydromethanopterin</a> to the cob(I)amide prosthetic group, and then from the cobamide to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a>. Only the latter transfer is sodium ion-dependent [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8223548">Stupperich93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8477726">Gartner93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7813469">Weiss94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7737157">Harms95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898900">Harms96a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9461302">Harms97</a>].
<p>
It has been proposed that methyl transfer from MtrA to coenzyme M is associated with a conformational change of the protein and that this change drives the electrogenic translocation of the sodium ions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11248186">Gottschalk01</a>]. The reaction starts with a methyl group transfer from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-THMPT"><i>N</i><sup>5</sup>-methyltetrahydromethanopterin</a> (methyl-H<sub>4</sub>MPT) bound to MtrH to the upper ligation site of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7162"><i>Co</i>&alpha;-[&alpha;-(5-hydroxybenzimidazolyl)]-cob(I)amide</a>, forming <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7163"><i>Co</i>&alpha;-[&alpha;-(5-hydroxybenzimidazolyl)]-<i>Co</i>&beta;-methylcob(III)amide</a>. The methyl group is subsequently transferred to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a> in the presence of sodium ions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8001564">Gartner94</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Methanogenesis from H<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub>, or acetate is dependent on the presence of sodium ions. The exergonic methyl transfer reaction is coupled to the endergonic pumping of sodium ions out of the cell, forming an ion gradient across the membrane. The two processes are catalyzed by a membrane-associated Na<sup>+</sup>-translocating/methyltranferase multienzyme complex composed of eight different subunits, MtrA-H. slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">Coenzyme M</a> is a small molecule consisting of sulfhydryl and sulfonate functional groups linked by an ethane moiety. It functions as a methyl carrier in methanogenic archaea, where it serves as the terminal intermediate of methanogenesis from all substrates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2115763">DiMarco90</a>].
<p>
In addition to its role in methanogenesis, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a> is used by some bacteria for the utilization of aliphtic alkenes, serving during ring opening of toxic epoxide intermediates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10411892">Allen99</a>].</comment>

slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
Methanogenesis, the biological production of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a>, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x10<sup>14</sup> g of methane per year.
<p>
Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=HYDROGEN-MOLECULE">H<SUB>2</SUB></a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FORMATE">formate</a>, and one of several alcohols, such as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETOH">ethanol</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ISO-PROPANOL">propan-2-ol</a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-326">butan-2-ol</a>, or <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7032">3-methylbutanol</a>. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METOH">methanol</a>, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides.
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">Acetate</a> is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METH-ACETATE-PWY">methanogenesis from acetate</a>). Most of the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> in nature originates from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a>.
<p>
Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHANOGENESIS-PWY">methanogenesis from H<SUB>2</SUB> and CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METH-ACETATE-PWY">methanogenesis from acetate</a>), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-8304">methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds</a>). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a>, forming <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a>, which is then disproportionated into <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>: One in four <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a> molecules is oxidized to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5209">methyl-coenzyme M oxidation to CO<sub>2</sub></a>), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a> molecules to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHFORM-PWY">methyl-coenzyme M reduction to methane</a>) [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bKeltjens93%5d">Keltjens93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15882413">Pritchett05</a>].
<p>
Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1282">CoB-CoM heterodisulfide</a>, which is produced during methane formation (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHFORM-PWY">methyl-coenzyme M reduction to methane</a>), is restored into <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1281">coenzyme B</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a> by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7105">F<sub>420</sub>H<sub>2</sub>:methanophenazine dehydrogenase</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7104">F<sub>420</sub> non-reducing hydrogenase I</a>), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5207">coenzyme B/coenzyme M regeneration I (methanophenazine-dependent)</a>). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes.
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
The process of methanogenesis from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> starts with activation of the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> by the unique cofactor <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Methanofurans" title="Methanofurans are a group of related carbon-carrier cofactors involved in the first step of the methanogenic reduction of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE''>CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> (see <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHANOGENESIS-PWY''>methanogenesis from H<SUB>2</SUB> and CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>). Methanofurans react with <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE''>CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> to form the carbamate <i>N</i>-carboxymethanofuran, which is reduced to <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Formyl-methanofurans''>a formylmethanofuran</a> by <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.2.7.12''>EC 1.2.7.12, formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase</a>.&#10;&#10;In addition, the cofactor also participates at a later stage of all methanogenesis pathways. These pathways converge at the compound <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM''>methyl-CoM</a>, which is then disproportionated into <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4''>methane</a> and <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE''>CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>; the latter process involves methanofuran (see <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5209''>methyl-coenzyme M oxidation to CO<sub>2</sub></a>).&#10;&#10;Methanofuran is also used by methylotrophic bacteria as a coenzyme to oxidize formaldehyde to formate [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9651254''>Chistoserdova98</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11532013''>Pomper01</a>].&#10;&#10;Methanofurans are the only cofactors known to contain a furan moiety, although furans have been identified in polyketides and fatty acid derived natural products, and are often formed during the heating or oxidation of carbohydrates [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12013276''>Graham02</a>].&#10;&#10;The chemical structure of methanofuran varies among different methanogens. At this time (2014) five variants have been characterized:&#10;<a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17181''>methanofuran a</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-145262''><i>Methanothermobacter thermautotrophicus</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1517208''>Eisenreich92</a>], <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7628''>methanofuran b</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2208''><i>Methanosarcina barkeri</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2883935''>Bobik87</a>], <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7629''>methanofuran c</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2173''><i>Methanobrevibacter smithii</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3170480''>White88a</a>], <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=methanofuran-d''>methanofuran d</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2190''><i>Methanocaldococcus jannaschii</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24977328''>Miller14</a>] and <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17182''>methanofuran e</a> (from <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-39152''><i>Methanococcus maripaludis</i></a>, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2187''><i>Methanococcus vannielii</i></a> and <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-155863''><i>Methanothermococcus okinawensis</i></a>) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25203397''>Allen14</a>].&#10;&#10;All methanofurans contain the basic core structure of 4-[<i>N</i>-&gamma;-L-glutamyl-&gamma;-L-glutamyl)-<i>p</i>-(&beta;-aminoethyl)phenoxymethyl]-2-(aminomethyl)furan, but with different attached side chains.">a methanofuran</a>, resulting in the formation of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Formyl-methanofurans">a formylmethanofuran</a>. The formyl group is then transferred to another cofactor, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THMPT">tetrahydromethanopterin</a>. A succession of transformations, catalyzed by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MCHMAUTO-MONOMER">methenyl-H<SUB>4</SUB>MPT cyclohydrolase</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=HMDMAUTO-MONOMER">H<SUB>2</SUB>-forming methylene-H<SUB>4</SUB>MPT dehydrogenase</a>, and finally <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MERMAUTO-MONOMER">F<SUB>420</SUB>-dependent methylene-H<SUB>4</SUB>MPT reductase</a>, which depends on the methanogenic cofactor <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Factor-420" title="One of the distinguishing features of methanogenic bacteria is their blue-green fluorescence when irradiated with UV light.&#10;&#10;<br> This fluorescence is due to F<sub>420</sub>, a flavin-related redox-active compound that is used as a cosubstrate by many enzymes in these organisms.&#10;&#10;While it is well-known for its role in methanogenesis, factor 420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium, where it assists in the synthesis of antibiotics like tetracycline and lincomycin. In addition, a modified form of the cofactor is also used by cyanobacteria in the repair of DNA damage.&#10;.&#10;Factor 420 (F<sub>420</sub>), named for its intense absorbance at 420 nm, was originally isolated by Cheeseman et al [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5079072''>Cheeseman72</a>], and later identified by Eirich et al as the N-(N-L-lactyl-&gamma;-L-glutamyl)-L-glutamic acid phosphodiester of 7,8-didemethyl-8-hydroxy-5-deazariboflavin 5'-phosphate [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/728375''>Eirich78</a>].&#10;&#10;The <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-8112''>F<sub>420</sub> biosynthetic pathway</a> produces the intermediate <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17242''>F<sub>420</sub>-0</a>, which contains no glutamate side chains. Glutamates are then added by several enzymes. F<sub>420</sub> molecules isolated from different organisms differ in the number of the glutamate molecules in the side chains, as well as the nature of the bond (which could be either &alpha; or &gamma;) [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11717263''>Choi01</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12909715''>Li03a</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12867481''>Graupner03</a>].">a factor 420</a>, results in the formation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-THMPT"><i>N</i><sup>5</sup>-methyltetrahydromethanopterin</a>. The methyl group is then transferred by
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-643">tetrahydromethanopterin <em>S</em>-methyltransferase complex</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a>, resulting in <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a>, which is then disproportionated into <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>, as described above.
<p>
Since only one in four <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a> molecules is oxidized to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>, providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of the other three <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a> molecules to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a>, the net reaction is conversion of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHFORM-PWY">methyl-coenzyme M reduction to methane</a>).</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">MtrA is the cobamide-binding subunit of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.1.1.86">EC 2.1.1.86, tetrahydromethanopterin <em>S</em>-methyltransferase</a>. More specifically, it binds a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7162"><i>Co</i>&alpha;-[&alpha;-(5-hydroxybenzimidazolyl)]-cob(I)amide</a> cofactor. It is membrane-associated, with a C-terminal transmembrane helix [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898900">Harms96a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9461302">Harms97</a>].
<p>
MtrA is not homologous to any known cobamide-binding proteins and is proposed as the motor of the sodium-ion pump. 
Genome analysis has revealed an extra copy or copies of the mtrA gene (named mtrA2) in many methanogenic archaea (e.g., <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-145263"><i>Methanothermobacter marburgensis</i></a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2162"><i>Methanobacterium formicicum</i></a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83816"><i>Methanobrevibacter ruminantium</i></a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2180"><i>Methanothermus fervidus</i></a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2208"><i>Methanosarcina barkeri</i></a>). These MtrA homologues encode cytoplasmic proteins that consist only of a soluble cobalamin-binding domain of 170-180 amino acids, which is in contrast to the approximately 250 amino acids of membrane-associated MtrA. MtrA homologues have also been identified in the genomes of some bacteria and non-methanogenic archaea.
<p>
Crystal structures are available for the soluble domain of MtrA from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2190"><i>Methanocaldococcus jannaschii</i></a> and the cytoplasmic MtrA homologue/cobalamin complex from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2180"><i>Methanothermus fervidus</i></a>. The MtrA fold was found to correspond to the Rossmann-type &alpha;/&beta; fold, which is also found in many cobalamin-containing proteins. However, the cobamide-binding site of MtrA differ greatly from all the other cobalamin-binding sites [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27324530">Wagner16</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Methanofurans are a group of related carbon-carrier cofactors involved in the first step of the methanogenic reduction of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHANOGENESIS-PWY">methanogenesis from H<SUB>2</SUB> and CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>). Methanofurans react with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> to form the carbamate <i>N</i>-carboxymethanofuran, which is reduced to <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Formyl-methanofurans">a formylmethanofuran</a> by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.2.7.12">EC 1.2.7.12, formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase</a>.
<p>
In addition, the cofactor also participates at a later stage of all methanogenesis pathways. These pathways converge at the compound <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a>, which is then disproportionated into <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>; the latter process involves methanofuran (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5209">methyl-coenzyme M oxidation to CO<sub>2</sub></a>).
<p>
Methanofuran is also used by methylotrophic bacteria as a coenzyme to oxidize formaldehyde to formate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9651254">Chistoserdova98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11532013">Pomper01</a>].
<p>
Methanofurans are the only cofactors known to contain a furan moiety, although furans have been identified in polyketides and fatty acid derived natural products, and are often formed during the heating or oxidation of carbohydrates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12013276">Graham02</a>].
<p>
The chemical structure of methanofuran varies among different methanogens. At this time (2014) five variants have been characterized:
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17181">methanofuran a</a> (from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-145262"><i>Methanothermobacter thermautotrophicus</i></a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1517208">Eisenreich92</a>], <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7628">methanofuran b</a> (from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2208"><i>Methanosarcina barkeri</i></a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2883935">Bobik87</a>], <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7629">methanofuran c</a> (from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2173"><i>Methanobrevibacter smithii</i></a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3170480">White88a</a>], <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=methanofuran-d">methanofuran d</a> (from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2190"><i>Methanocaldococcus jannaschii</i></a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24977328">Miller14</a>] and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17182">methanofuran e</a> (from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-39152"><i>Methanococcus maripaludis</i></a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2187"><i>Methanococcus vannielii</i></a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-155863"><i>Methanothermococcus okinawensis</i></a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25203397">Allen14</a>].
<p>
All methanofurans contain the basic core structure of 4-[<i>N</i>-&gamma;-L-glutamyl-&gamma;-L-glutamyl)-<i>p</i>-(&beta;-aminoethyl)phenoxymethyl]-2-(aminomethyl)furan, but with different attached side chains.</comment>

slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">One of the distinguishing features of methanogenic bacteria is their blue-green fluorescence when irradiated with UV light.

<br> This fluorescence is due to F<sub>420</sub>, a flavin-related redox-active compound that is used as a cosubstrate by many enzymes in these organisms.
<p>
While it is well-known for its role in methanogenesis, factor 420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium, where it assists in the synthesis of antibiotics like tetracycline and lincomycin. In addition, a modified form of the cofactor is also used by cyanobacteria in the repair of DNA damage.
.
Factor 420 (F<sub>420</sub>), named for its intense absorbance at 420 nm, was originally isolated by Cheeseman et al [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5079072">Cheeseman72</a>], and later identified by Eirich et al as the N-(N-L-lactyl-&gamma;-L-glutamyl)-L-glutamic acid phosphodiester of 7,8-didemethyl-8-hydroxy-5-deazariboflavin 5'-phosphate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/728375">Eirich78</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-8112">F<sub>420</sub> biosynthetic pathway</a> produces the intermediate <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17242">F<sub>420</sub>-0</a>, which contains no glutamate side chains. Glutamates are then added by several enzymes. F<sub>420</sub> molecules isolated from different organisms differ in the number of the glutamate molecules in the side chains, as well as the nature of the bond (which could be either &alpha; or &gamma;) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11717263">Choi01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12909715">Li03a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12867481">Graupner03</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10763">Methanopterin</a> is one of several modified folates that have been identified in Archaea [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6319137">vanBeelen84</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2624671">RaemakersFranke89</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1910453">RaemakersFranke91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1915350">RaemakersFranke91a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8501071">White93</a>] (see also <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10764">sarcinapterin</a>). While common in all methanogenic archaea, some C1-oxidizing members of the domain Bacteria also contain an <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THMPT">tetrahydromethanopterin</a>-related carrier, which they use in energy metabolism (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-1723">formaldehyde oxidation VI (H<sub>4</sub>MPT pathway)</a>).
<p>
Serving a similar role to the one that folates serve in bacteria and eukaryotes, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10763">methanopterin</a> carries C1 (single
carbon) fragments between formyl and methyl oxidation levels (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHANOGENESIS-PWY">methanogenesis from H<SUB>2</SUB> and CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>). Despite the similarities, there are clear differences between <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THF">tetrahydrofolate</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THMPT">tetrahydromethanopterin</a>. In the reductive direction, ATP is consumed in the entry of carbon from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> into the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THF">tetrahydrofolate</a> pathway, but not in entry into the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THMPT">tetrahydromethanopterin</a> pathway.
<p>
In the oxidative direction, methyl groups are much more readily oxidized on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THMPT">tetrahydromethanopterin</a> than on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THF">tetrahydrofolate</a>. Moreover, the redox reactions on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THMPT">tetrahydromethanopterin</a> are coupled to more negative reductants than the pyridine nucleotides which are used in the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=THF">tetrahydrofolate</a> pathway [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10970772">Maden00</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Arsenic is the most prevalent environmental toxic substance. It ranks first on the priority list of Hazardous Substances published by the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR), based on a combination of frequency, toxicity, and potential for human exposure. It is also a Group 1 human carcinogen associated with skin, bladder and lung cancer.
<p>
While arsenic exists in two oxidation states, As(III) and As(V), in aerobic environments most inorganic arsenic is found as As(V), such as arsenic acid. The prevalent form of arsenic acid under neutral pH is <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ARSENATE">arsenate<sup>2-</sup></a>.
<p>
At neutral pH values arsenate exists mostly in the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ARSENATE">AsO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup></a> form (pKa<sup>1</sup>= 2:3; pKa<sup>2</sup> = 6:8; and pKa<sup>3</sup> = 11:6) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11161507">Goldberg01</a>].
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ARSENATE">Arsenate</a> is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters most cells via phosphate transporters. Once inside cells, arsenate is removed by assorted detoxification mechanisms, described in pathways under <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ECOCYC-CLASS&object=Arsenate-Detoxification" title="This class contains pathways for arsenate detoxification">Arsenate Detoxification</a>.</comment>

slots.xml: <comment datatype="string">The &beta; subunit contains an intact A cluster that encompasses a binuclear Ni-Ni center bridged by a cysteine thiolate to an [Fe4S4] cluster. Acetyl transfer from acetyl-CoA generates a &beta; subunit acetyl-enzyme intermediate. In the process of acetyl-enzyme formation, reductive activation of the &beta; subunit A cluster involves the uptake of two electrons, added in two separate one-electron steps [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20202935">Gencic10</a>].</comment>
