slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-461">acetyl-CoA decarbonylase/synthase complex</a> (ACDS) is an important enzyme in the methanogenesis pathway from acetate. It cleaves the C-C and C-S bonds in the acetyl moiety of acetyl-CoA, oxidizes the carbonyl group to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> and transfers the methyl group to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-8">tetrahydrosarcinapterin</a>. The enzyme can also catalyze the synthesis of acetyl-CoA, a reaction that is not used in methanogenesis, but in autotrophic growth on one-carbon substrates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3023296">Terlesky86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2824458">Terlesky87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2123865">Abbanat90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1512186">Ferry92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8955306">MaupinFurlow96</a>].
<p>
This large (~2000 kDa) complex is composed of three enzyme components and five different subunits, with a structure of (&alpha;<sub>2</sub>&epsilon;<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(&beta;)<sub>8</sub>(&gamma;&delta;)<sub>8</sub>.
<p>
The &beta; subunit contains a binuclear Ni-Ni center bridged by a cysteine thiolate to an [Fe4S4] cluster [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10600570">Kocsis99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12464601">Gencic03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14664578">Gu03a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14709073">Funk04</a>], and the &gamma;&delta; component contains a corrinoid/iron-sulfur cofactor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8550451">MaupinFurlow96a</a>].
<p>
Several partial reactions were correlated with specific components of the complex [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626532">Grahame96</a>]: CO dehydrogenase activity (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=1.2.7.4-RXN">EC 1.2.7.4</a>) is catalyzed by the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-443">&alpha;&epsilon; component</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18621675">Gong08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12657792">Balbo03</a>], carbon monoxide-methylating acetyl-CoA synthase activity (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=ACETYLSYNCLTH-RXN">EC 2.3.1.169</a>) is catalyzed by the &beta; subunit, and the rapid, reversible transfer of a methyl group between the &gamma;&delta; component's corrinoid cofactor and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-8">tetrahydrosarcinapterin</a> (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=RXN-12908">EC 2.1.1.245</a>) is catalyzed by the &gamma;&delta; component.
<p>
The enzyme components and the reactions catalyzed by them are similar to the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-1302">carbon monoxide dehydrogenase/acetyl-CoA synthase</a> enzyme system, which is used for anaerobic oxidation of acetate by anaerobic bacteria and for <i>de novo</i> synthesis of acetyl groups in autotrophic species and acetogens. However, that system includes several individual enzymes that, unlike ACDS, are isolated separately and not present in the form of a high molecular mass complex [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20202935">Gencic10</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The corrinoid iron-sulfur protein (CoFeSP) is functional in the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=CODH-PWY">reductive acetyl coenzyme A pathway I (homoacetogenic bacteria)</a> of autotrophic carbon fixation in various bacteria and archaea, where it is essential for the biosynthesis of acetyl-CoA.
<p>
The protein from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-129958"><i>Carboxydothermus hydrogenoformans</i></a> contains two cofactors - <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Co-a-5-methoxy-benzimidazole-cobamides" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides''>A cobamide</a> is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20843''>cobamide</a>, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=COBINAMIDE''>cob(I)inamide</a> by the attachment of an &alpha;-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain.&#10;&#10;Biologically active forms of cobamides contain an upper (&beta;) and a lower (&alpha;) axial ligands. The most common upper axial ligand are either a methyl group or a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group, although some other forms exist. More variability is found with the lower axial ligand, where more that 16 different forms have been described. This class includes all cobamides that have a 5-methoxy-6-methylbenzimidazole group as their lower axial ligand.">5-methoxybenzimidazolylcobamide</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-7" title="Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways.&#10;Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure.  The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. &#10;&#10;Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3.&#10;&#10;In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates and are thus classified as enzyme cofactors. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.8.1.8''>EC 2.8.1.8, lipoyl synthase</a>, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29051382''>McCarthy17</a>].">a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. The cobamide is bound in a base-off state, with neither the 5-methoxybenzimidazolyl group nor a nitrogen atom from a protein side chain coordinating the cobalt [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16983091">Svetlitchnaia06</a>].
<p>
CoFeSP acts in two methylation reactions: the transfer of a methyl group from methyltransferase-bound methyltetrahydrofolate to the cob(I)amide of CoFeSP, during which the cobalt is oxidized to the (III) state (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.1.1.258">EC 2.1.1.258, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate&mdash;corrinoid/iron-sulfur protein <em>Co</em>-methyltransferase</a>), and the transfer of the methyl group of methyl-cob(III)amide to the reduced Ni-Ni-[4Fe-4S] active site cluster of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.3.1.169">EC 2.3.1.169, CO-methylating acetyl-CoA synthase</a>, during which the cobalt is restored to its active (I) state [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16983091">Svetlitchnaia06</a>].
<p>
More recent findings suggest that the protein may also be involved as a methyl donor in methionine biosynthesis by MesB-type core methionine synthases [<a href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.04.21.054031v2">Price20</a>].
<p>
The protein is heterodimeric, consisting of two tightly interacting subunits. The large subunit, encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-80944">acsC</a> gene, comprises three domains, of which the N-terminal domain binds the [4Fe-4S] cluster, the middle domain is a (&beta;&alpha;)<sub>8</sub>-barrel, and the C-terminal domain shows an open fold and binds Cobeta-aqua-(5,6-dimethylbenzimidazolylcobamide) in a "base-off" state without a protein ligand at the cobalt ion. The small subunit, encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-80945">acsD</a> gene, also displays a (&beta;&alpha;)<sub>8</sub>-barrel fold and interacts with the upper side of the corrin macrocycle [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16983091">Svetlitchnaia06</a>].
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Corrinoids are a group of compounds based on the skeleton of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Corrins" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Corrins''>Corrin</a> is a macrocycle related to the porphyrin ring. The 4 pyrrole subunits in a corrin are joined on opposite sides by a C-CH3 methylene link and on one side by a C-H methylene link, and two of the pyrroles are joined directly. Compared to a porphyrin, the corrin is missing a bridging methylene group between a pair of pyrroles.&#10;Corrinoids usually complex a cobalt atom, as seen in cobalamin.&#10;&#10;Compound that contain a corrin ring are called <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Corrinoids''>corrinoids</a>.">corrin</a>, a cyclic system containing four pyrrole rings similar to porphyrins. They often contain a cobalt atom. 
<p>
"Corrinoid proteins" are proteins that bind corrinoid cofactors. The most common corrinoid proteins are methyltransferases and reductive dehalogenases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8631705">Tallant96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8932317">Paul96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11976751">Neumann02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17142327">Hagemeier06</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
Methanogenesis, the biological production of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a>, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x10<sup>14</sup> g of methane per year.
<p>
Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=HYDROGEN-MOLECULE">H<SUB>2</SUB></a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FORMATE">formate</a>, and one of several alcohols, such as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETOH">ethanol</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ISO-PROPANOL">propan-2-ol</a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-326">butan-2-ol</a>, or <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-7032">3-methylbutanol</a>. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METOH">methanol</a>, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides.
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">Acetate</a> is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METH-ACETATE-PWY">methanogenesis from acetate</a>). Most of the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> in nature originates from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a>.
<p>
Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHANOGENESIS-PWY">methanogenesis from H<SUB>2</SUB> and CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METH-ACETATE-PWY">methanogenesis from acetate</a>), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-8304">methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds</a>). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a>, forming <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a>, which is then disproportionated into <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>: One in four <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a> molecules is oxidized to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5209">methyl-coenzyme M oxidation to CO<sub>2</sub></a>), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a> molecules to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHFORM-PWY">methyl-coenzyme M reduction to methane</a>) [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bKeltjens93%5d">Keltjens93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15882413">Pritchett05</a>].
<p>
Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1282">CoB-CoM heterodisulfide</a>, which is produced during methane formation (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHFORM-PWY">methyl-coenzyme M reduction to methane</a>), is restored into <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1281">coenzyme B</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a> by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7105">F<sub>420</sub>H<sub>2</sub>:methanophenazine dehydrogenase</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7104">F<sub>420</sub> non-reducing hydrogenase I</a>), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5207">coenzyme B/coenzyme M regeneration I (methanophenazine-dependent)</a>). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes.
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
Although most of the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> in nature originates from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a>, only two genera of methanogenic acetotrophs are known: the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2207"><i>Methanosarcina</i></a> and the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2222"><i>Methanothrix</i></a>.
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">Acetate</a> is phosphorylated and activated to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a>, which is then processed by a large enzyme complex, known as the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-461">acetyl-CoA decarbonylase/synthase complex</a>.
This enzyme complex cleaves the C-C and C-S bonds in the acetyl moiety of acetyl-CoA, oxidizes the carbonyl group to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> and transfers the methyl group to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-8">tetrahydrosarcinapterin</a>. The enzyme can also catalyze the synthesis of acetyl-CoA, a reaction that is not used in methanogenesis, but for autotrophic growth on one-carbon substrates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3023296">Terlesky86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2824458">Terlesky87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2123865">Abbanat90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1512186">Ferry92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8955306">MaupinFurlow96</a>].
<p>
The large (~2000 kDa) complex is composed of three enzyme components and five different subunits, with a structure of (&alpha;<sub>2</sub>&epsilon;<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(&beta;)<sub>8</sub>(&gamma;&delta;)<sub>8</sub>.
The specific components of the complex catalyze several partial reactions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626532">Grahame96</a>]: CO dehydrogenase activity (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=1.2.7.4-RXN">EC 1.2.7.4</a>) is catalyzed by the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-443">&alpha;&epsilon; component</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18621675">Gong08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12657792">Balbo03</a>], acetyl-CoA:corrinoid protein Co-methyltransferas activity, along with CO production (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=ACETYLSYNCLTH-RXN">EC 2.3.1.169</a>) is catalyzed by the &beta; subunit, and the rapid, reversible transfer of a methyl group between the &gamma;&delta; component's corrinoid cofactor and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-8">tetrahydrosarcinapterin</a> (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=RXN-12908">EC 2.1.1.cj</a>) is catalyzed by the &gamma;&delta; component.
<p>
The methyl group, which has been transferred to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-8">tetrahydrosarcinapterin</a>, is then transferred to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a> producing <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Me-CoM">methyl-CoM</a>, which is reductively demethylated to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CH4">methane</a> with electrons from <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1281">coenzyme B</a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=METHFORM-PWY">methyl-coenzyme M reduction to methane</a>).
<p>
The resulting heterodisulfides of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CoM">coenzyme M</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1281">coenzyme B</a> are then reduced to their sulfhydryl forms (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5207">coenzyme B/coenzyme M regeneration I (methanophenazine-dependent)</a>) [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bFerry93%5d">Ferry93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1512186">Ferry92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9782487">Thauer98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9233537">Ferry97</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Corrinoid iron-sulfur proteins (CoFeSP) are functional in the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=CODH-PWY">reductive acetyl coenzyme A pathway I (homoacetogenic bacteria)</a> of autotrophic carbon fixation in various bacteria and archaea, where they are essential for the biosynthesis of acetyl-CoA.
<p>
The protein from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-129958"><i>Carboxydothermus hydrogenoformans</i></a> contains two cofactors - <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Co-a-5-methoxy-benzimidazole-cobamides" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides''>A cobamide</a> is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20843''>cobamide</a>, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=COBINAMIDE''>cob(I)inamide</a> by the attachment of an &alpha;-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain.&#10;&#10;Biologically active forms of cobamides contain an upper (&beta;) and a lower (&alpha;) axial ligands. The most common upper axial ligand are either a methyl group or a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group, although some other forms exist. More variability is found with the lower axial ligand, where more that 16 different forms have been described. This class includes all cobamides that have a 5-methoxy-6-methylbenzimidazole group as their lower axial ligand.">5-methoxybenzimidazolylcobamide</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-7" title="Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways.&#10;Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure.  The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. &#10;&#10;Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3.&#10;&#10;In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates and are thus classified as enzyme cofactors. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.8.1.8''>EC 2.8.1.8, lipoyl synthase</a>, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29051382''>McCarthy17</a>].">a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. The cobamide is bound in a base-off state, with neither the 5-methoxybenzimidazolyl group nor a nitrogen atom from a protein side chain coordinating the cobalt [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16983091">Svetlitchnaia06</a>].
<p>
CoFeSP acts in two methylation reactions: the transfer of a methyl group from methyltransferase-bound methyltetrahydrofolate to the cob(I)amide of CoFeSP, during which the cobalt is oxidized to the (III) state (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.1.1.258">EC 2.1.1.258, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate&mdash;corrinoid/iron-sulfur protein <em>Co</em>-methyltransferase</a>), and the transfer of the methyl group of methyl-cob(III)amide to the reduced Ni-Ni-[4Fe-4S] active site cluster of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.3.1.169">EC 2.3.1.169, CO-methylating acetyl-CoA synthase</a>, during which the cobalt is restored to its active (I) state [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16983091">Svetlitchnaia06</a>].
<p>
More recent findings suggest that the protein may also be involved as a methyl donor in methionine biosynthesis by MesB-type core methionine synthases [<a href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.04.21.054031v2">Price20</a>].
<p>
The protein is heterodimeric, consisting of two tightly interacting subunits. The large CfsA subunit comprises three domains, of which the N-terminal domain binds the [4Fe-4S] cluster, the middle domain is a (&beta;&alpha;)<sub>8</sub>-barrel, and the C-terminal domain shows an open fold and binds Cobeta-aqua-(5,6-dimethylbenzimidazolylcobamide) in a "base-off" state without a protein ligand at the cobalt ion. The small CfsB subunit also displays a (&beta;&alpha;)<sub>8</sub>-barrel fold and interacts with the upper side of the corrin macrocycle [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16983091">Svetlitchnaia06</a>].
</comment>

projection.label: predicted structural protein, ethanolamine utilization microcompartment

slots.name: common-name
slots.xml: <common-name datatype="string">predicted structural protein, ethanolamine utilization microcompartment</common-name>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The EutL protein resembles carboxysomal shell proteins and is thought to form a proteinaceous membrane that confines a microcompartment for ethanolamine ammonia-lyase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19451619">Sagermann09</a>].  The flat, cyclic pseudohexameric structure with a central pore may be a basic building block for a microcompartment shell [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>].  The pore structure can be triggered to open upon exposure to zinc [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20851901">Takenoya10</a>].
<p>
Crystal structures of EutL have been solved at 2.2 &Aring; [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19194002">Nikolakakis09</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19451619">Sagermann09</a>], 2.3 &Aring; [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>] and 2.6 &Aring; [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20851901">Takenoya10</a>] resolution.  The structures show that the protein is arranged in a hexagonal trimeric structure, with the monomers arranged around a large central pore that is either closed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19451619">Sagermann09</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>] or open [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20851901">Takenoya10</a>].  In solution, EutL initially elutes as a trimer during size-exclusion chromatography, but forms larger complexes at lower pH or by longer incubation time after cell lysis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19451619">Sagermann09</a>].
<p>
The functions of the orthologous <i>eut</i> operon genes for ethanolamine utilization in <i>Salmonella typhimurium</i> have been studied experimentally [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>].
<p>
A <i>eutL</i> up allele increases fitness during growth in medium containing lignocellulosic hydrolysate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20639866">Warner10</a>].
<p>
Comment: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044564">Kang10c</a>]
</comment>

projection.label: putative ethanolamine catabolic microcompartment shell protein EutM

slots.name: common-name
slots.xml: <common-name datatype="string">putative ethanolamine catabolic microcompartment shell protein EutM</common-name>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The EutM protein resembles carboxysomal shell proteins and can form a 2-dimensional protein membrane with an architecture that is similar to EutL.  Unlike EutL, the pore structure of EutM appears positively charged [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20851901">Takenoya10</a>].
<p>
Crystal structures of EutM have been determined at 2.1 &Aring; [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>], 2.7 &Aring; and 2.0 &Aring; [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20851901">Takenoya10</a>] resolution.  The &alpha;/&beta; structure resembles that of carboxysomal shell proteins.  The flat, cyclic hexameric structure with a central pore may be a basic building block for a microcompartment shell [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20851901">Takenoya10</a>].
<p>
The functions of the orthologous <i>eut</i> operon genes for ethanolamine utilization in <i>Salmonella enterica</i> have been studied experimentally [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>].
<p>
Comment: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044564">Kang10c</a>]</comment>

projection.label: putative ethanolamine catabolic microcompartment shell protein EutS

slots.name: common-name
slots.xml: <common-name datatype="string">putative ethanolamine catabolic microcompartment shell protein EutS</common-name>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The crystal structure of EutS has been determined at 1.65 &Aring; resolution.  The &alpha;/&beta; structure resembles that of carboxysomal shell proteins, although the cyclic hexameric structure has a bend of approximately 40&deg;.  This may allow formation of the edges of a polyhedral microcompartment shell [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>].
<p>
A G39V mutant protein forms a flat, symmetric hexameric structure [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>].
<p>
The functions of the orthologous <i>eut</i> operon genes for ethanolamine utilization in <i>Salmonella enterica</i> have been studied experimentally [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The EutD protein has phosphotransacetylase activity.  Expression of EutD - either from a plasmid or by inducing expression of the <i>eut</i> operon with ethanolamine and vitamin B12 - can rescue the growth defect of a <i>pta acs</i> mutant for growth on acetate as the sole source of carbon [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21046341">Bologna10</a>].
<p>
<i>eutD</i> shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes.  It was therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response.  A <i>eutD</i> deletion mutant was shown to be more sensitive than wild-type specifically to heat shock, but not other stresses [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24580753">Krisko14</a>].
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Ethanolamine ammonia-lyase (EAL) allows <i>E. coli</i> to utilize ethanolamine as the sole source of nitrogen and carbon in the presence of external vitamin B<sub>12</sub> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1090845">Chang75b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6374020">Jones84b</a>].  EAL is an adenosylcobalamin-dependent enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319195">Blackwell77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33657">Blackwell78</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19762342">Akita10</a>] that is spontaneously inactivated by its substrate and can be reactivated by EutA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15466038">Mori04</a>].  The enzyme was first studied in the non-K-12 strain NCIB 8114 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319195">Blackwell77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33657">Blackwell78</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/371614">Blackwell78a</a>].  
<p>
Crystal structures of an N-terminally truncated, but active form of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19762342">Akita10</a>] both in binary and ternary complexes with the cofactor and substrate have been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20516606">Shibata10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20519496">Shibata10a</a>].  The enzyme is composed of a hexamer of (&alpha;&beta;)<sub>2</sub> dimers, with the &alpha; subunit holding the active site and the cobalamin cofactor bound at the interface between the &alpha; and &beta; subunits [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20519496">Shibata10a</a>].  The authors propose a reaction mechanism that is consistent with a previously described mechanism for adenosylcobalamin-dependent rearrangements [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3076429">Babior88</a>].  The stereochemical course of the reaction has been modeled on the basis of crystal structures, accounting for the apparent lack of stereospecificity of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21142024">Shibata11</a>].
<p>
Production of EAL is catabolite repressed and is induced by the simultaneous presence of ethanolamine and the adenosylcobalamin cofactor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319195">Blackwell77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/371614">Blackwell78a</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The EutK protein consists of a BMC (bacterial microcompartment)-type domain followed by an additional C-terminal helix-turn-helix domain. Unlike the other BMC-type proteins (EutL, EutM and EutS), it behaves as a monomer in solution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>].
<p>
The crystal structure of the C-terminal domain of EutK has been determined at 2.1 &Aring; resolution. This domain forms a helix-turn-helix structure, suggesting that EutK binds nucleic acids [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20044574">Tanaka10a</a>].
<p>
The function of the orthologous <i>eut</i> operon genes for ethanolamine utilization in <i>Salmonella typhimurium</i> have been studied experimentally [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>].
<p>
Expression of <i>eutK</i> does not change under anaerobiosis but decreases in an <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PD00197">FNR</a> mutant strain (MC4100 &Delta;<i>fnr-2</i>) compared to wild type; an FNR binding site is predicted upstream of <i>eutK</i>, but its location is not precisely identified [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12754220">Salmon03</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">EutA is the reactivating factor for <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=ETHAMLY-CPLX">ethanolamine ammonia-lyase</a> (EAL).  EAL is one of a group of adenosylcobalamin-dependent enzymes which undergo suicide inactivation during catalysis and inactivation in the absence of substrate.  Reactivation of EAL by EutA takes place in the presence of ATP, Mg<sup>2+</sup> and free adenosylcobalamin, and EutA appears to be the sole enzyme responsible for this reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15466038">Mori04</a>].
<p>
EutA: "<b>e</b>thanolamine <b>ut</b>ilization <b>A</b>"</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml: <comment datatype="string">Sequence analysis has identified EutH as a membrane protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7868611">Stojiljkovic95a</a>] with 11 transmembrane helices [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>].  A possible ethanolamine transport function for EutH has been suggested [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7868611">Stojiljkovic95a</a>]. Although it was initially found that a <i>eutH</i> mutant in <i>Salmonella enterica</i> is not defective for ethanolamine utilization [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>], further studies showed a pH-dependent effect, and it is now thought that EutH facilitates diffusion of protonated ethanolamine across the cytoplasmic membrane [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15466042">Penrod04</a>].</comment>

slots.name: common-name
slots.xml: <common-name datatype="string">putative ethanolamine catabolic microcompartment shell protein EutN</common-name>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Several genes of the <i>eut</i> operon are involved in the ability to utilize ethanolamine as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen in <i>Salmonella typhimurium</i>; the operon is conserved between <i>Salmonella</i> and <i>E. coli</i>.  EutN has not been shown to be involved in ethanolamine utilization in either <i>Salmonella</i> or <i>E. coli</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>].  EutN is similar to the carboxysomal shell protein CcmL of <i>Synechococcus</i> sp. strain PCC7942 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8491708">Price93a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>].
<p>
A crystal structure of EutN has been solved at 2.4 &Aring; resolution.  The protein forms a tight hexamer with a central hole that is predominantly covered by acidic residues, suggesting a pore with a transport function [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17588214">Forouhar07</a>].
<p>
EutN: "<b>e</b>thanolamine <b>ut</b>ilization"
<p>
CchB: "<b>c</b>arbon dioxide <b>c</b>oncentration <b>h</b>omolog <b>B</b>" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7868611">Stojiljkovic95a</a>]</comment>

gene may be mutated (the rationale is that EV-IMP is used where an
abnormal situation prevails in a cell or organism).

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Vitamin B12 was discovered in the 1920s after Minot and Murphy reported that they could cure the
symptoms of pernicious anaemia by feeding patients with crude liver extract (they received the
Nobel prize in 1934 for this discovery) [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bMinot26%5d">Minot26</a>].
The mysterious factor has been isolated and subsequently crystallized in 1948 [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bLester48%5d">Smith48</a>, <a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bRickes48%5d">Rickes48</a>],
and was given the name vitamin B12 and, as it was shown to contain a cobalt ion, cobalamin [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12195810">Warren02a</a>]. 
<p>
Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> is one of the most structurally complex small molecules
made in Nature. It contains a contracted porphinoid ring with a cobalt ion ligated at its center,
and further held in place by a lower axial base (a dimethylbenzimidazole) and an upper methyl or
(as in this case) adenosyl group.
<p>
While no eukaryote is able to make cobalamin, the archae and certain eubacteria possess the
genes that encode the thirty plus cobalamin biosynthetic enzymes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12195810">Warren02a</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Cobalamin is the term used for <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides''>A cobamide</a> is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20843''>cobamide</a>, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=COBINAMIDE''>cob(I)inamide</a> by the attachment of an &alpha;-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain. Cobamides serve as cofactors for a number of important enzymes.&#10;&#10;A key structural feature of cobinamides is a corrin ring with a cobalt ion in its center. Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamide-Upper-Ligands''>upper</a> (&beta;) and <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamide-Lower-Ligands''>lower</a> (&alpha;) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. The best known cobamide, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobalamins''>cobalamin</a>, contains <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE''>5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a> as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand.&#10;&#10;At least 16 different cobamides with structural variability in the lower ligand have been described. The 16 bases reported so far are <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZIMIDAZOLE''>benzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18320''>5-methylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18321''>5-methoxybenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18497''>5-hydroxybenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18495''>5-methoxy-6-methylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE''>5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENINE''>adenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18323''>2-methyladenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=GUANINE''>guanine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=HYPOXANTHINE''>hypoxanthine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=PHENOL''>phenol</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-108''>4-methylphenol</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-5723''>2-(methylsulfanyl)adenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20865''>2-methylsulfonyladenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20864''>2-methylsulfinyladenine</a>, and <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20885''>naphthimidazole</a>  [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24055007''>Crofts13</a>]. Different cobamides may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14351147''>Ford55</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13796808''>Barker60</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13796809''>Barker60a</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21696461''>Chan11</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22923412''>Yi12b</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23417488''>Mok13</a>].">a cobamide</a> where the cobalt ion is attached to a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE">5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a> lower axial ligand, without specifying the upper axial ligand. It includes several compounds often referred to as vitamin B12, that differ in the upper axial ligand. The functional forms of the B12 vitamin, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-9037">methylcob(III)alamin</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a>, include either a methyl group or an 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as their upper axial ligand, respectively.
<p>
Other forms of cobalamin include <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a> (or its conjugated acid <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AQUACOBIIIALAMIN">aquacobalamin</a>) and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a>. <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">Hydroxocobalamin</a> is a naturally produced form synthesized by many bacterial species, while <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a> is a common semi-synthetic form produced from bacterially-synthesized <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a>. Vitamin B12 pills often contain <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a>, which is converted to the active forms in the body.
<p>
The cobalt ion embedded in cobalamin may exist in different charges (+1, +2 or +3), and the different forms of the compound are referred to as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COB-I-ALAMIN">cob(I)alamin</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17105">cob(III)alamin</a>, respectively.</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Cobalamin is the term used for <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides''>A cobamide</a> is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20843''>cobamide</a>, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=COBINAMIDE''>cob(I)inamide</a> by the attachment of an &alpha;-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain. Cobamides serve as cofactors for a number of important enzymes.&#10;&#10;A key structural feature of cobinamides is a corrin ring with a cobalt ion in its center. Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamide-Upper-Ligands''>upper</a> (&beta;) and <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamide-Lower-Ligands''>lower</a> (&alpha;) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. The best known cobamide, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobalamins''>cobalamin</a>, contains <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE''>5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a> as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand.&#10;&#10;At least 16 different cobamides with structural variability in the lower ligand have been described. The 16 bases reported so far are <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZIMIDAZOLE''>benzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18320''>5-methylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18321''>5-methoxybenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18497''>5-hydroxybenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18495''>5-methoxy-6-methylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE''>5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENINE''>adenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18323''>2-methyladenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=GUANINE''>guanine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=HYPOXANTHINE''>hypoxanthine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=PHENOL''>phenol</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-108''>4-methylphenol</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-5723''>2-(methylsulfanyl)adenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20865''>2-methylsulfonyladenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20864''>2-methylsulfinyladenine</a>, and <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20885''>naphthimidazole</a>  [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24055007''>Crofts13</a>]. Different cobamides may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14351147''>Ford55</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13796808''>Barker60</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13796809''>Barker60a</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21696461''>Chan11</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22923412''>Yi12b</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23417488''>Mok13</a>].">a cobamide</a> attached to a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE">5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a> lower axial ligand of the cobalt ion, without specifying the upper axial ligand. It includes several compounds often referred to as vitamin B12, that differ in the upper axial ligand. The functional forms of the B12 vitamin, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-9037">methylcob(III)alamin</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a>, include either a methyl group or an 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as their upper axial ligand, respectively.
<p>
Other forms of cobalamin include <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a> (or its conjugated acid <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AQUACOBIIIALAMIN">aquacobalamin</a>) and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a>. <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">Hydroxocobalamin</a> is a naturally produced form synthesized by many bacterial species, while <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a> is a common semi-synthetic form produced from bacterially-synthesized <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a>. Vitamin B12 pills often contain <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a>, which is converted to the active forms in the body.
<p>
The cobalt ion embedded in cobalamin may exist in different charges (+1, +2 or +3), and the different forms of the compound are referred to as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COB-I-ALAMIN">cob(I)alamin</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17105">cob(III)alamin</a>, respectively.
<p>
Cyanocob(III)alamin is a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17105">cob(III)alamin</a> derivative where the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CO%2b3">Co<sup>3+</sup></a> ion is held in place partly due to an upper cyano group. The cyano group is an artificial ligand, created as a result of the extraction procedure. It is converted in mammals to active forms of cobalamin by the action of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.16.1.6">EC 1.16.1.6, cyanocobalamin reductase</a>.</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Cobalamin is the term used for <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamides''>A cobamide</a> is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20843''>cobamide</a>, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=COBINAMIDE''>cob(I)inamide</a> by the attachment of an &alpha;-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain. Cobamides serve as cofactors for a number of important enzymes.&#10;&#10;A key structural feature of cobinamides is a corrin ring with a cobalt ion in its center. Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamide-Upper-Ligands''>upper</a> (&beta;) and <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobamide-Lower-Ligands''>lower</a> (&alpha;) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. The best known cobamide, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cobalamins''>cobalamin</a>, contains <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE''>5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a> as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand.&#10;&#10;At least 16 different cobamides with structural variability in the lower ligand have been described. The 16 bases reported so far are <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZIMIDAZOLE''>benzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18320''>5-methylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18321''>5-methoxybenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18497''>5-hydroxybenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18495''>5-methoxy-6-methylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE''>5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENINE''>adenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-18323''>2-methyladenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=GUANINE''>guanine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=HYPOXANTHINE''>hypoxanthine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=PHENOL''>phenol</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-108''>4-methylphenol</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-5723''>2-(methylsulfanyl)adenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20865''>2-methylsulfonyladenine</a>, <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20864''>2-methylsulfinyladenine</a>, and <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-20885''>naphthimidazole</a>  [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24055007''>Crofts13</a>]. Different cobamides may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14351147''>Ford55</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13796808''>Barker60</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13796809''>Barker60a</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21696461''>Chan11</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22923412''>Yi12b</a>, <a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23417488''>Mok13</a>].">a cobamide</a> attached to a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE">5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a> lower axial ligand of the cobalt ion, without specifying the upper axial ligand. It includes several compounds often referred to as vitamin B12, that differ in the upper axial ligand. The functional forms of the B12 vitamin, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-9037">methylcob(III)alamin</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a>, include either a methyl group or an 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as their upper axial ligand, respectively.
<p>
Other forms of cobalamin include <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a> (or its conjugated acid <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AQUACOBIIIALAMIN">aquacobalamin</a>) and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a>. <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">Hydroxocobalamin</a> is a naturally produced form synthesized by many bacterial species, while <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a> is a common semi-synthetic form produced from bacterially-synthesized <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a>. Vitamin B12 pills often contain <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a>, which is converted to the active forms in the body.
<p>
The cobalt ion embedded in cobalamin may exist in different charges (+1, +2 or +3), and the different forms of the compound are referred to as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COB-I-ALAMIN">cob(I)alamin</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-17105">cob(III)alamin</a>, respectively.</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a> degrades <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> by a pathway dependent on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a>, a required cofactor of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-4.3.1.7">EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase</a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY0-1477">ethanolamine utilization</a>). The ethanolamine utilization (<i>eut</i>) operon includes all the genes that are necessary for the conversion of inactive cobalamins, such as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">vitamin B<sub>12</sub></a>, to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a>. One of these genes is <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2467">eutT</a>, which encodes an <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.5.1.154">EC 2.5.1.154, corrinoid adenosyltransferase EutT</a>.
<p>
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a> possesses three adenosyltransferases that show no obvious amino acid sequence similarity. <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13220">corrinoid adenosyltransferase CobA</a> is the housekeeping enzyme, and participates in the <i>de novo</i> biosynthesis of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a> as well as the recycling of cobinamides. <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2050">PduO</a> is involved in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-7013">(<i>S</i>)-propane-1,2-diol degradation</a>, and is only induced in the presence of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PROPANE-1-2-DIOL">(<i>S</i>)-propane-1,2-diol</a>. Similarly, EutT participates in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY0-1477">ethanolamine utilization</a> and is induced only in the presence of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a>. Its main role is to convert inactive cobalamins to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a> specifically for the use of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-4.3.1.7">EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase</a>.
<p>
The actual substrate for the enzymatic reaction is <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COB-I-ALAMIN">cob(I)alamin</a>, in which the cobalt ion has a valency of +1. However, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COB-I-ALAMIN">cob(I)alamin</a> is very reactive, and, if left unprotected, is rapidly oxidized to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a>. The midpoint redox potential of the Co<sup>2+</sup>/Co<sup>1+</sup> couple is -610 mV, which is is too low for any known cellular reductant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4489">Lexa76</a>].
Remarkably, the enzyme is able to overcome this thermodynamic barrier. After binding <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a> an <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PHE">L-phenylalanine</a> residue displaces the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE">5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole</a> lower ligand [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19236001">Mera09</a>], generating a four-coordinate <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a> intermediate, the reduction potential of which is higher by >250 mV, bringing it within physiological range [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15954777">Stich05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15913339">Stich05a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18672897">Park08b</a>]. The cobalt is subsequently reduced to the +1 valence. The source of the electron used for the reduction of the enzyme-bound <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COB-I-ALAMIN">cob(I)alamin</a> <i>in vivo</i> has not been established. However, CobA was shown to interact <i>in vitro</i> with flavodoxin A (FldA), and reduced FldA was shown to efficiently drive the adenosylation of cob(II)alamin [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11408479">Fonseca01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16207720">Buan05</a>]. Furthermore, free reduced flavins and non-specific flavoproteins can also reduce cob(II)alamin bound in the active site of the enzyme, leading to the suggestion that bona fide cobalamin reductases may not be necessary [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19933577">Mera10</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2467">eutT</a> gene was cloned and expressed in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, and the recombinant protein was partially purified. Extracts of strains expressing the gene were assayed in the presence of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a>, ATP, and titanium(III) citrate (which reduces <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1256">hydroxocobalamin</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COB-I-ALAMIN">cob(I)alamin</a>), and  showed 50- to 100-fold more adenosyltransferase activity than the control strain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15516577">Sheppard04</a>].
<p>
In a subsequent study the enzyme was overproduced and enriched to approximately 70% homogeneity. The enzyme, which was produced as insoluble inclusion bodies, was solubilized by detergent, and its basic kinetic parameters were determined. Unlike CobA, EutT does not adenosylate either <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=COBINAMIDE">cob(I)inamide</a> or <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-315">cyanocob(III)alamin</a>. In addition, while PduO and CobA eliminate the tripolyphosphate group of ATP as <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=P3I">triphosphate</a>, EutT produces <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PPI">diphosphate</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=Pi">phosphate</a>, and is not inhibited by <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=P3I">triphosphate</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16636051">Buan06</a>].
<p>
A later study managed to purify the enzyme to homogeneity in the absence of detergents. The gene was cloned with an N-terminal hexahistidine tag and a maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag in tandem and expressed in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>. The recombinant protein was purified under anaerobic conditions, and the tags were subsequently removed.The purified enzyme converted <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-1829">cob(II)alamin</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a> in the presence of free dihydroflavins and ATP. The enzyme contained zinc, which is likely bound to a HX11CCXXC motif. However, the highest activity was observed with Fe(II) ions, and it was suggested that iron, rather than zinc, acts <i>in vivo</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24336938">Moore14</a>].
<p>
It is believed that following the completion of the reaction, the enzyme interacts with the target protein, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-4.3.1.7">EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase</a>, to ensure proper delivery of the cofactor. The concentrations of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a> are too low for simple diffusion. While this has not been shown for this enzyme, a similar phenomenon was demonstrated for a PduO enzyme from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-408"><i>Methylorubrum extorquens</i></a>, which transfers adenosylcobalamin directly to methylmalonyl-CoA mutase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18264093">Padovani08</a>]</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The EutD protein has phosphotransacetylase activity.  Expression of EutD - either from a plasmid or by inducing expression of the <i>eut</i> operon with ethanolamine and vitamin B12 - can rescue the growth defect of a <i>pta acs</i> mutant for growth on acetate as the sole source of carbon [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21046341">Bologna10</a>].
<p>
<i>eutD</i> shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes.  It was therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response.  A <i>eutD</i> deletion mutant was shown to be more sensitive than wild-type specifically to heat shock, but not other stresses [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24580753">Krisko14</a>].
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">Ethanolamine ammonia-lyase (EAL) allows <i>E. coli</i> to utilize ethanolamine as the sole source of nitrogen and carbon in the presence of external vitamin B<sub>12</sub> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1090845">Chang75b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6374020">Jones84b</a>].  EAL is an adenosylcobalamin-dependent enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319195">Blackwell77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33657">Blackwell78</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19762342">Akita10</a>] that is spontaneously inactivated by its substrate and can be reactivated by EutA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15466038">Mori04</a>].  The enzyme was first studied in the non-K-12 strain NCIB 8114 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319195">Blackwell77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33657">Blackwell78</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/371614">Blackwell78a</a>].  
<p>
Crystal structures of an N-terminally truncated, but active form of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19762342">Akita10</a>] both in binary and ternary complexes with the cofactor and substrate have been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20516606">Shibata10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20519496">Shibata10a</a>].  The enzyme is composed of a hexamer of (&alpha;&beta;)<sub>2</sub> dimers, with the &alpha; subunit holding the active site and the cobalamin cofactor bound at the interface between the &alpha; and &beta; subunits [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20519496">Shibata10a</a>].  The authors propose a reaction mechanism that is consistent with a previously described mechanism for adenosylcobalamin-dependent rearrangements [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3076429">Babior88</a>].  The stereochemical course of the reaction has been modeled on the basis of crystal structures, accounting for the apparent lack of stereospecificity of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21142024">Shibata11</a>].
<p>
Production of EAL is catabolite repressed and is induced by the simultaneous presence of ethanolamine and the adenosylcobalamin cofactor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319195">Blackwell77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/371614">Blackwell78a</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <i>eut</i> operon, characterized from enteric bacteria such as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a>, encodes enzymes required for the catabolism of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> and its use as a carbon, nitrogen, and energy source [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1090845">Chang75b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/784902">Scarlett76</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6374020">Jones84b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7868611">Stojiljkovic95a</a>].
<p>
In these organisms the pathway occur within the lumen of a bacterial microcompartment (MPC) known as the <i>eut</i> metabolosome, a capsid-like shell composed of multiple proteins that is analogous to the carboxysome of cyanobacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>]. A similar compartment is used by these organsisms for the catabolism of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PROPANE-1-2-DIOL">(<i>S</i>)-propane-1,2-diol</a> (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-7013">(<i>S</i>)-propane-1,2-diol degradation</a>). The metabolosome serves several functions - it protects the cells from the toxicity of the acetaldehyde intermediate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16291677">Brinsmade05</a>]; it prevent carbon loss from volatilization of acetaldehyde [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>]; and it makes it easier to recycle cofactors used in ethanolamine catabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23585538">Huseby13</a>]. The <i>eut</i> operon, whose expression is induced by the presence of ethanolamine and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a>, encodes all functions needed for the assembly and function of the metabolosome, as well as the enzymes of the3 pathway [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464203">Kofoid99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23920494">Held13</a>]. Full <i>eut</i> operons have been found in Enterobacteriaceae, Firmicutes, Nocardioides sp., and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-851"><i>Fusobacterium nucleatum</i></a>. It should be noted that many other organisms contain a much shorter operon that often includes only the genes encoding the first enzyme of the pathway, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-4.3.1.7">EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19783625">Tsoy09</a>].
<p>
In the intestine, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> is derived from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE" title="Phosphatidylethanolamines are a class of <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Phosphoglycerides''>phosphoglycerolipids</a> found in biological membranes. They are synthesized by the addition of an ethanolamine group from CDP-ethanolamine to <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Diacylglycerides''>diglycerides</a>.&#10;&#10;Phosphatidylethanolamines are found in all living cells, composing 25% of all phospholipids.">phosphatidylethanolamine</a>, a major component of eukaryotic membranes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4888138">Fung69</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6304089">Larson83</a>]. Use of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> as a carbon or nitrogen source requires <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a>, which serves as the cofactor of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-4.3.1.7">EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase</a> and a coinducer (with ethanolamine) of the <i>eut</i> operon transcription. While <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, which is not capable of producing <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN">adenosylcobalamin</a> <i>de novo</i>, requires an external source of the cofactor, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a> can produce it under anaerobic conditions. It has been shown that one of the genes of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a> operon, <i>eutT</i>, encodes <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.5.1.17">EC 2.5.1.17, corrinoid adenosyltransferase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15516577">Sheppard04</a>].
<p>
The operon also includes the <i>eutE</i> gene, which is assumed to encode <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.2.1.10">EC 1.2.1.10, acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acetylating)</a>, and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G7288">eutD</a>, which encodes the next enzyme in the pathway, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.3.1.8">EC 2.3.1.8, phosphate acetyltransferase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14996820">Brinsmade04</a>].
<p>
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2461">eutG</a> gene of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a> is located in the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> utilization operon, and encodes a 391-amino-acid protein with a strong similarity to several characterized alcohol dehydrogenases. Sequence analysis also suggested that the enzyme binds iron and uses an NAD coenzyme.
<p>
A &Delta;<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2461">eutG</a> strain grew at pH 7 or below, but not at pH 8, and released more <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETALD">acetaldehyde</a> than wild-type cells during growth on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLYCEROL">glycerol</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a>. The mutant was not able to grow with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> as the sole carbon source [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>]. 
<p>
The phenotype was corrected by providing a different carbon source, suggesting that EutG helps to conserve or use <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETALD">acetaldehyde</a> rather than removing a toxic accumulation. The authors speculated that EutG may simply serve to help recycle electron carriers and balance redox reactions during fermentation, by converting excess acetaldehyde to ethanol and NADH to NAD [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>].
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2469">eutP</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2468">eutQ</a> genes of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a> are located next to each other in the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> utilization operon. Bioinformatics analyses show that EutQ belongs to the cupin superfamily, which includes a wide variety of enzymes such as carbohydrate-binding isomerases, flavonoid-binding dioxygenases and nuclear factors.
<p>
A &Delta;<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2468">eutQ</a> strain released <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETALD">acetaldehyde</a> into the medium during growth on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLYCEROL">glycerol</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>]. When the mutant was grown under anaerobic conditions with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> as the main carbon source (a small amount of glycerol was also included) and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-14">tetrathionate</a> (40 mM) as the terminal electron acceptor, growth stop after consumption of the glycerol. Growth inhibition was not observed if a gene encoding <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.2.1.10">EC 1.2.1.10, acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acetylating)</a> was introduced and expressed at a high level, indicating that the growth inhibition was due to accumulation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETALD">acetaldehyde</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26448059">Moore16</a>].
<p>
The authors suspected that the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2468">eutQ</a> gene may encode an acetate kinase. To test this hypothesis, several other genes encoding acetate kinase were introduced into the mutant, resulting in each case in restored anoxic growth of the mutant on ethanolamine and tetrathionate. The opposite was also true - overexpressing <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2468">eutQ</a> in a &Delta;ackA strain corrected its growth defect [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26448059">Moore16</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2469">eutP</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2468">eutQ</a> genes were cloned with a poly His tag and expressed in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, and the recombinant proteins were purified to homogeneity. The purified proteins were assayed <i>in vitro</i> in the opposite direction, and both catalyzed the production of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a> and ATP when provided with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-P">acetyl phosphate</a> and ADP. When either protein was assayed in a coupled reacction with purified EutD and acetyl-CoA, both formed ATP and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a>, indicating that they are indeed acetate kinases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26448059">Moore16</a>].
<p>
While the location of the proteins is not known yet, the fact that they are specifically encoded by the <i>eut</i> operon suggests that they are localized within the metabolosome.
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2469">eutP</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2468">eutQ</a> genes of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28901"><i>Salmonella enterica</i></a> are located next to each other in the <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> utilization operon. Bioinformatics analyses show that EutP is a member of the P-loop containing nucleoside triphosphate hydrolase superfamily.
<p>
A &Delta;<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2469">eutP</a> strain released <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETALD">acetaldehyde</a> into the medium during growth on <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLYCEROL">glycerol</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16585748">Penrod06</a>]. However, when the mutant was grown under anaerobic conditions with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ETHANOL-AMINE">ethanolamine</a> as the main carbon source (a small amount of glycerol was also included) and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-14">tetrathionate</a> (40 mM) as the terminal electron acceptor, no phenotype was observed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26448059">Moore16</a>].
<p>
The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2469">eutP</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=STM2468">eutQ</a> genes were cloned with a poly His tag and expressed in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, and the recombinant proteins were purified to homogeneity. The purified proteins were assayed <i>in vitro</i> for acetate kinase activity in the opposite direction, and both catalyzed the production of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a> and ATP when provided with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-P">acetyl phosphate</a> and ADP. When either protein was assayed in a coupled reacction with purified EutD and acetyl-CoA, both formed ATP and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACET">acetate</a>, indicating that they are indeed acetate kinases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26448059">Moore16</a>].
<p>
While the location of the proteins is not known yet, the fact that they are specifically encoded by the <i>eut</i> operon suggests that they are localized within the metabolosome.
</comment>
